unit-m3u4.title: Unit 3 · Lesson 4: Multiply 2-Digit by 2-Digit Numbers
unit-m3u4.source: enVision Topic 3 textbook scan — Multiply Multi-Digit Whole Numbers (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 3-4 of the Topic 3 textbook scan: multiplying a 2-digit number by a 2-digit number with an area model, partial products and the standard algorithm.

why.text: Two-digit by two-digit is where the placeholder zero first appears, and it is the step most students drop.

objectives.text: Multiply 2-digit by 2-digit numbers with an area model
Multiply 2-digit by 2-digit numbers with the standard algorithm
Explain the placeholder zero in the second row
See the standard algorithm as a shortcut for partial products

parentNote.text: Two mistakes are built into the wrong options on purpose. Leaving the zero off the second row (34 × 26 → 272) and multiplying only tens-by-tens and ones-by-ones (43 × 25 → 815, missing the two "cross" pieces). Both give answers that are wildly off from an estimate, which is exactly why every explanation here ends with one.

nextUp.text: Two rows, and the second row always starts with a 0.

cards.def:
**Split both factors into tens and ones and find all four partial products.**
• 23 × 45: 20 × 40 = 800, 20 × 5 = 100, 3 × 40 = 120, 3 × 5 = 15.
• 800 + 100 + 120 + 15 = 1,035.
cards.hint: Two parts times two parts makes four pieces.

cards.term: Two rows in the standard algorithm
cards.def:
**First multiply by the ones digit, then by the tens digit, then add the two rows.**
• 34 × 26: row 1 is 34 × 6 = 204. Row 2 is 34 × 20 = 680.
• 204 + 680 = 884.
cards.hint: One row for the ones, one row for the tens.

cards.def:
**The second row starts with a 0 because you are multiplying by TENS.**
• In 34 × 26 the 2 means 20, so the row is 680, not 68.
cards.hint: Tens row → zero in the ones place first.

cards.def:
**The two rows ARE partial products, with some of them already added together.**
• Row 1 is (ones digit) × the whole number; row 2 is (tens digit) × the whole number.

**Round both factors and multiply.**
• 57 × 18 is about 60 × 20 = 1,200, so 1,026 is reasonable.
cards.hint: Close to the estimate? Good. Far off? Look again.

questions.q: Which set of partial products gives 23 × 45?

ex.main: **800, 100, 120 and 15.** Each tens-or-ones part of 23 meets each part of 45, making four pieces.
ex.tip: 800 and 15 alone leave out the two "cross" pieces — a very common gap.

questions.q: In the standard algorithm for 34 × 26, why does the second row start with a 0?
opts: Because 34 × 2 has a zero in it
Because that row multiplies 34 by 2 tens
Because every row in multiplication ends in 0
Because you must always add a zero to be neat
questions.hint: What does the 2 in 26 stand for?
steps: The zero shows the row is worth tens.

ex.main: **Because that row multiplies 34 by 2 tens.** 34 × 20 = 680, and the 0 holds the ones place.
ex.tip: Leaving the 0 off turns 680 into 68 and shrinks the answer badly.
272 leaves the zero off the second row. 624 only multiplies tens by tens and ones by ones.
Estimate: 60 × 20 = 1,200. 513 is far too small — the second row lost its zero.
Estimate: 40 × 20 = 800, so an answer a bit over 800 makes sense.

questions.q: A ferry carries 36 cars each trip. It makes 28 trips. How many cars does it carry?
questions.hint: Multiply the cars per trip by the number of trips.

ex.main: **1,008 cars.** The two rows are 288 and 720.
ex.tip: 64 comes from adding 36 and 28 — "each trip" means multiply.

questions.q: A café is open 24 hours a day for 31 days. How many hours is it open?
questions.hint: Multiply hours per day by the number of days.

ex.tip: Estimate: 25 × 30 = 750 — very close. 96 leaves the zero off the tens row.

questions.q: A student found 43 × 25 by doing 40 × 20 = 800 and 3 × 5 = 15, then got 815. What was left out?
opts: A zero at the end of the answer
Only the regrouping in the ones place
questions.hint: Draw the area model. How many pieces should there be?

ex.main: **The two cross pieces, 40 × 5 and 3 × 20.** The full product is 1,075.
ex.tip: Estimate: 40 × 25 = 1,000, so 815 was too small to be right.

questions.q: A bus holds 35 adults or 48 children. It makes 26 full trips. How many more people ride if every trip carries children instead of adults?
questions.hint: Find how many more fit on ONE trip first.
steps: Each trip carries 48 − 35 = 13 more children than adults.

ex.main: **338 more people.** 13 extra per trip, times 26 trips.
ex.tip: 1,248 is the total number of children — the question asks how many MORE.

questions.q: Janet says the standard algorithm is just a shortcut for partial products. Is she right?
opts: No — the standard algorithm gives a different answer from partial products
Yes — each row is a partial product, and the rows are added at the end
No — partial products only work when both numbers are small ones
Yes — but only when neither factor needs any regrouping at all
steps: Those are partial products — each row just combines two of the four area-model pieces.

ex.main: **Yes.** Each row is a partial product, so both methods add up the same pieces.
ex.tip: That is why you can check one method with the other.
